subject: science
name: Exploring Mixtures and their Separation
summary: Most materials around us are mixtures. Mixtures can be homogeneous or heterogeneous, and by particle size they are solutions, colloids or suspensions. We express how much solute is in a solution by concentration and solubility, and we separate mixtures using differences in properties — crystallisation, distillation, chromatography, separating funnels, sublimation, filtration, centrifugation and coagulation. Colloids show the Tyndall effect, and alloys are solid solutions.

topics.title: Pure substances, mixtures and particle size
topics.summary: A pure substance has one kind of particle and fixed properties; a mixture has two or more substances not chemically combined. Mixtures are homogeneous or heterogeneous, and by particle size are solutions (< 1 nm), colloids (1–1000 nm) or suspensions (> 1000 nm).
topics.simple: A **pure substance** is made of only one kind of particle — like distilled water or gold. A **mixture** has two or more substances just mixed, not chemically joined — like lemonade or sand in water. If a mixture looks the same everywhere, it is **homogeneous**; if you can see different parts, it is **heterogeneous**.
topics.explain:
**Pure substance:** made of a single kind of particle (an element or a compound). It has a fixed composition and fixed properties, such as a definite melting and boiling point. Examples: distilled water, sugar, copper, oxygen.

**Mixture:** two or more substances mixed physically, **not chemically combined**.
- Composition can **vary** (you can make tea stronger or weaker)
- Each component **keeps its own properties**
- Components can be separated by **physical methods**

**Types of mixtures:**
- **Homogeneous:** uniform composition throughout; you cannot see separate parts. Examples: salt solution, sugar in water, air, brass.
- **Heterogeneous:** non-uniform; different parts can be seen or detected. Examples: sand in water, oil in water, a fruit salad, muddy water.

**Classifying by particle size** (1 nm = one billionth of a metre):
- **Solution:** particles smaller than **1 nm** — homogeneous, clear, particles never settle, pass through filter paper. E.g. salt water.
- **Colloid:** particles between **1 nm and 1000 nm** — look uniform but are actually heterogeneous; particles don't settle and pass through filter paper; scatter light. E.g. milk.
- **Suspension:** particles larger than **1000 nm** — heterogeneous, often visible, settle on standing, can be removed by filtration. E.g. muddy water, chalk in water.
topics.example: Stir sugar, milk powder and chalk powder into three glasses of water. The sugar water stays clear and never settles (solution); the milk looks uniform but cloudy (colloid); the chalk makes the water cloudy and slowly sinks to the bottom (suspension).
keyPoints: Pure substance: one kind of particle, fixed properties
Mixture: components not chemically combined; variable composition; separable physically
Homogeneous = uniform; heterogeneous = visible parts
Solution < 1 nm; colloid 1–1000 nm; suspension > 1000 nm
Only suspension particles settle and get filtered out

topics.title: Solutions and concentration
topics.summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute in solvent; its concentration can be given as % mass by mass, % mass by volume or % volume by volume.
topics.simple: In a solution, the substance that dissolves is the **solute** (like sugar) and the substance it dissolves in is the **solvent** (like water). **Concentration** tells how much solute is present in a certain amount of solution — like how strong or weak your nimbu-paani is.
topics.explain:
**Solution:** a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
- **Solute:** the component present in smaller amount that gets dissolved (e.g. salt)
- **Solvent:** the component present in larger amount that dissolves the solute (e.g. water)
- Water dissolves so many substances that it is called a **universal solvent**.
- Solutions can be solid, liquid or gas: air (gases in gas), soda water (CO₂ gas in water), alloys (solid in solid).

**Concentration** — the amount of solute in a given amount of solution.

1. **Mass by mass percentage (% m/m)**
= (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100
Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.

2. **Mass by volume percentage (% m/v)**
= (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100

3. **Volume by volume percentage (% v/v)** — for a liquid dissolved in a liquid
= (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100

**Worked example (% m/m):** 10 g of salt is dissolved in 90 g of water.
- Mass of solution = 10 + 90 = 100 g
- % m/m = (10 ÷ 100) × 100 = **10%**

**Worked example (% m/m):** 20 g of sugar in 180 g of water.
- Mass of solution = 200 g → (20 ÷ 200) × 100 = **10%**

**Worked example (% m/v):** 5 g of glucose dissolved to make 100 mL of solution → (5 ÷ 100) × 100 = **5% m/v**

**Worked example (% v/v):** 25 mL of ethanol is mixed with water to make 250 mL of solution → (25 ÷ 250) × 100 = **10% v/v**
topics.example: ORS or a glucose drip in hospitals is labelled with its concentration. A '5% glucose' drip has 5 g of glucose in every 100 mL of solution (% m/v).
keyPoints: Solute dissolves in the solvent; solute is usually the smaller part
Water = universal solvent
% m/m = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100
% m/v = (g of solute ÷ mL of solution) × 100
% v/v = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100
Divide by mass of SOLUTION (solute + solvent), not solvent alone

topics.title: Solubility, saturated solutions and crystallisation
topics.summary: Solubility is the maximum grams of solute that dissolve in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature; most solids dissolve more when hot, gases less. Cooling a hot saturated solution slowly gives pure crystals (crystallisation).
topics.simple: There is a limit to how much sugar you can dissolve in a glass of water. When no more will dissolve, the solution is **saturated**. Hot water can usually hold more solid than cold water. If a hot saturated solution cools slowly, the extra solid comes out as neat, pure **crystals**.
topics.explain:
**Solubility:** the maximum mass of a solute (in grams) that can dissolve in **100 g of solvent** at a particular temperature.
- Example: about **36 g** of common salt dissolves in 100 g of water at room temperature (about 20 °C).

**Saturated solution:** holds the maximum solute it can at that temperature; extra solute stays undissolved.
**Unsaturated solution:** can still dissolve more solute at that temperature.

**Effect of temperature:**
- **Most solids** become **more soluble** as temperature rises (sugar dissolves faster and more in hot tea).
- **Gases** become **less soluble** as temperature rises — warm cold drinks go flat, and fish in warm water get less dissolved oxygen.
- Some solids (like common salt) change their solubility only a little with temperature.

**Solubility curves:** graphs of solubility (y-axis) against temperature (x-axis). A steep curve means solubility changes a lot with temperature. From a curve you can read how much solute dissolves at any temperature, or how much will crystallise out when a solution is cooled.

**Crystallisation:** a method to get a **pure solid** from its solution.
1. Make a hot, saturated solution of the impure solid and filter it.
2. Let it **cool slowly**. The solubility drops, so the extra solute separates as crystals.
3. Filter off the crystals and dry them.

**Why crystallisation is better than evaporation:**
- Some solids **decompose or char** when heated to dryness (e.g. sugar).
- Soluble impurities stay dissolved in the leftover liquid instead of drying onto the product.
- Slow cooling gives large, well-formed, **pure** crystals.
Crystallisation is used to purify salt from sea water and to make alum and copper sulphate crystals.
topics.example:
Solubility of salt ≈ 36 g per 100 g water at 20 °C. How much salt can dissolve in 50 g of water at 20 °C?
- 100 g water → 36 g salt
- 50 g water → 36 × 50/100 = **18 g**
keyPoints: Solubility = max g of solute per 100 g solvent at a given temperature
Saturated: can't dissolve more; unsaturated: can
Most solids: more soluble when hot
Gases: less soluble when hot
Solubility curve = solubility vs temperature graph
Crystallisation: slow cooling of hot saturated solution → pure crystals
Better than evaporation: no charring, impurities stay in solution

topics.title: Distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography
topics.summary: Distillation separates miscible liquids whose boiling points differ by 25 °C or more; fractional distillation is used when the difference is less than 25 °C. Paper chromatography separates coloured components like inks and dyes.
topics.simple: To separate two liquids that are fully mixed, heat the mixture: the liquid that boils first turns to vapour, which is cooled back into liquid in a separate container — that's **distillation**. To separate colours in an ink, put a dot on paper and let a solvent climb up the paper: different colours travel different distances — that's **chromatography**.
topics.explain:
**Distillation** — separates two **miscible** liquids (liquids that mix completely) that **do not decompose on boiling**, when their **boiling points differ by about 25 °C or more**.
- The mixture is heated; the liquid with the **lower boiling point** vaporises first.
- The vapour passes through a **condenser** (cooled by water), turns back to liquid and is collected as the **distillate**.
- The higher-boiling liquid is left behind.
- Example: **acetone (boiling point 56 °C) and water (100 °C)** — acetone distils over first.

**Fractional distillation** — used when boiling points differ by **less than 25 °C**.
- A **fractionating column** (packed with glass beads) is fitted between the flask and condenser. It gives the vapours a large surface to repeatedly condense and re-vaporise, so the liquids separate better.
- Uses: separating the gases of air (after liquefying air), petroleum into its fractions, and ethanol from water.

**Traditional distillation — deg-bhapka (Kannauj, Uttar Pradesh):** perfumers of Kannauj make natural perfumes called **attars** by an age-old method. Flowers and water are heated in a large copper pot (**deg**) over a fire. The fragrant steam travels through a bamboo pipe into a receiver (**bhapka**) kept in cool water, usually containing a base oil such as sandalwood oil, which traps the fragrance.

**Paper chromatography** — separates **small amounts of coloured substances** dissolved in the same solvent.
1. Put a small spot of ink on a strip of filter paper, a little above the bottom.
2. Dip the bottom edge in a solvent (water or alcohol), keeping the **spot above the solvent level** — otherwise the spot would simply dissolve into the solvent in the jar.
3. The solvent rises up the paper and carries the dyes with it. Components that dissolve more readily and stick less to the paper move higher.
4. The ink splits into separate coloured bands.
Uses: separating dyes in inks and pigments from plants.
topics.example: Put a black sketch-pen dot on a strip of filter paper and dip its end in water (dot above the water). Within minutes you may see bands of blue, purple and yellow — black ink is often a mixture of dyes.
keyPoints: Distillation: miscible liquids, boiling points differ by ≥ 25 °C
Lower-boiling liquid vaporises first, condenses in condenser
Acetone (56 °C) + water (100 °C) → simple distillation
Fractional distillation: difference < 25 °C; uses a fractionating column
Kannauj attars: deg (copper still) and bhapka (receiver with sandalwood oil)
Chromatography: spot must be above solvent level
Separates dyes in ink, plant pigments

topics.title: Separating suspensions and other mixtures
topics.summary: Immiscible liquids are separated with a separating funnel, sublimable solids by sublimation, and suspensions by settling, filtration, centrifugation or coagulation with alum.
topics.simple: Oil and water don't mix, so a **separating funnel** lets you drain off the lower water layer. Camphor and naphthalene turn straight from solid to vapour, so they can be separated by **sublimation**. Mud in water can be filtered, spun fast (**centrifugation**) or made to clump and sink by adding **alum**.
topics.explain:
**Separating funnel** — for **immiscible liquids** (liquids that don't mix and form layers).
- The denser liquid forms the **lower layer**.
- In a mixture of **water and mustard oil**, oil is less dense, so **water is the lower layer** and **mustard oil the upper layer**.
- Opening the stopcock lets the lower layer (water) run out first; close it when the oil reaches the tap.

**Sublimation** — some solids change directly from solid to vapour on heating (and back to solid on cooling) without becoming liquid. Examples: **camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride**.
- To separate salt and ammonium chloride: heat the mixture in a china dish covered with an inverted funnel; ammonium chloride vapour collects as solid on the cool funnel walls, and salt stays behind.

**Separating suspensions:**
- **Sedimentation and decantation:** let heavier particles settle, then pour off the liquid.
- **Filtration:** pass the mixture through filter paper or cloth; the solid (**residue**) stays on it and the liquid (**filtrate**) passes through. Straining tea leaves is filtration.
- **Centrifugation:** spinning the mixture very fast forces the denser particles to the bottom (outward), and the lighter part collects on top. Uses: separating **cream from milk** (dairies, and the butter-making process), separating blood cells from plasma in **blood tests**, drying clothes in a washing machine. A low-cost hand-powered **paperfuge**, made of paper and string, spins fast enough to separate blood components where there is no electricity.
- **Coagulation / loading with alum:** adding **alum** (*phitkari*) to muddy water makes tiny suspended particles clump into bigger, heavier lumps that settle quickly. This 'loading' is an old Indian way to clear water.
- **Paneer from milk:** adding lemon juice or vinegar to hot milk makes the milk proteins coagulate into solid lumps; filtering through a muslin cloth separates the paneer from the liquid whey.
topics.example: At home, when making ghee or buttermilk, the cream can be separated quickly by churning; in dairies, large centrifuges separate cream from milk. In villages, a piece of alum swirled in a pot of muddy river water makes the mud settle overnight.
keyPoints: Separating funnel: immiscible liquids; denser liquid below
Water (lower) + mustard oil (upper)
Sublimation: camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride
Filtration: residue stays, filtrate passes
Centrifugation: cream from milk, blood tests; paperfuge
Alum makes suspended particles clump and settle (loading)
Paneer: milk proteins coagulated by lemon juice, filtered

topics.title: Colloids, emulsions and the Tyndall effect
topics.summary: A colloid has a dispersed phase spread through a dispersion medium; emulsions are liquid-in-liquid colloids (oil-in-water or water-in-oil); colloids scatter a beam of light (Tyndall effect), while true solutions do not.
topics.simple: In a **colloid**, tiny particles of one substance are spread throughout another but are too small to see or to settle. Milk, fog, smoke and jelly are colloids. Shine a torch through a colloid and you can see the beam's path, because the particles scatter light — this is the **Tyndall effect**.
topics.explain:
A **colloid** has two parts:
- **Dispersed phase:** the substance present as tiny particles (1–1000 nm)
- **Dispersion medium:** the substance in which they are spread

**Properties of colloids:**
- Appear homogeneous but are actually **heterogeneous**
- Particles are too small to see with the eye
- Particles **do not settle** on standing and **pass through filter paper** (they can be separated by centrifugation)
- They **scatter light** (Tyndall effect)

**Examples by type:**
- **Fog, mist, clouds:** liquid droplets in gas (aerosol)
- **Smoke:** solid particles in gas
- **Gel** (jelly, cheese): liquid dispersed in a solid
- **Foam** (shaving cream, whipped cream): gas in liquid
- **Emulsion:** liquid in liquid

**Emulsions:**
- **Oil-in-water:** tiny oil droplets spread in water. Examples: **milk**, **vanishing cream**.
- **Water-in-oil:** tiny water droplets spread in oil or fat. Examples: **butter**, **cold cream**.
- An **emulsifier** (like soap or egg yolk) helps keep an emulsion from separating.

**Tyndall effect** (named after the scientist **John Tyndall**): the **scattering of a beam of light by colloid particles**, making the path of the beam visible.
- Seen in colloids (and suspensions), **not in true solutions**, because solution particles are too small to scatter light noticeably.
- Everyday examples: sunlight streaming through gaps in a forest canopy on a misty morning, a torch or car headlight beam in fog, a beam of light entering a dark, dusty room or cinema hall.
- A simple test: shine a torch through salt water (beam not seen) and through dilute milk (beam clearly seen).
topics.example: In a dark room, shine a laser pointer or torch through a glass of salt water and a glass of water with a few drops of milk. The beam is invisible in the salt solution but shows up as a bright line in the milky water — the Tyndall effect.
keyPoints: Colloid = dispersed phase + dispersion medium
Particles 1–1000 nm; don't settle; pass through filter paper
Oil-in-water: milk, vanishing cream
Water-in-oil: butter, cold cream
Fog, smoke, gel, foam are colloids
Tyndall effect (John Tyndall): colloid particles scatter light
True solutions do not show the Tyndall effect

topics.title: Alloys and choosing a separation technique
topics.summary: Alloys are solid solutions of metals (with other metals or non-metals), e.g. brass, bronze, stainless steel and solder. The right separation technique depends on the properties that differ between the components.
topics.simple: An **alloy** is a metal mixed evenly with other metals or with a non-metal, like brass (copper + zinc). It is a solid solution. To separate any mixture, look for a property in which the parts differ — size, boiling point, solubility, density, magnetism — and choose the method that uses that difference.
topics.explain:
**Alloys** are homogeneous mixtures — **solid solutions** — of a metal with other metals or a non-metal. They are mixtures because their composition can vary and they show properties of their components, yet the parts cannot be separated by simple physical methods like filtration.

Alloys are made to improve properties such as strength, hardness and resistance to rusting.
- **Brass:** copper and zinc (about 80% copper, 20% zinc) — utensils, taps, musical instruments, idols
- **Bronze:** copper and tin — statues, medals, bells
- **Stainless steel:** iron with chromium, nickel and a little carbon — does not rust; kitchen utensils, surgical tools
- **Solder:** lead and tin — low melting point; used to join electrical wires

**Choosing a separation technique** — match the method to the property that differs:
- Insoluble solid in a liquid → **filtration** (or sedimentation and decantation)
- Very fine or light suspended particles → **centrifugation** or **coagulation with alum**
- Soluble solid from a liquid, pure solid wanted → **crystallisation** (or evaporation if the solid doesn't decompose)
- Two miscible liquids, boiling points differ by ≥ 25 °C → **distillation**
- Miscible liquids, boiling points differ by < 25 °C → **fractional distillation**
- Two immiscible liquids → **separating funnel**
- One component sublimes → **sublimation**
- Several coloured dyes in a solution → **chromatography**
- One component magnetic (iron filings) → **magnet**

Often a mixture needs **several steps**. For salt + sand + ammonium chloride: sublime off the ammonium chloride, dissolve the rest in water and filter out the sand, then evaporate or crystallise to get the salt.
topics.example: Separating a mixture of salt, sand and water: filter to remove sand (residue); then evaporate or crystallise the salt from the filtrate. If you also want the water, distil the filtrate instead of evaporating it.
keyPoints: Alloys = solid solutions (homogeneous mixtures)
Brass: copper + zinc; bronze: copper + tin
Stainless steel: iron + chromium + nickel + carbon
Solder: lead + tin (low melting point)
Choose method by differing property: size, solubility, boiling point, density, sublimation, magnetism
Complex mixtures need several steps

Separating coloured components (like dyes in ink) as a solvent carries them different distances along paper.
Separating particles by spinning a mixture fast so denser particles move to the bottom.
A mixture with particles 1–1000 nm (dispersed phase) spread through a dispersion medium; does not settle and scatters light.
Scattering of a light beam by colloid particles, making the beam's path visible; not shown by true solutions.
A solid solution of a metal with other metals or a non-metal, e.g. brass, bronze, stainless steel, solder.

formulas: Mass by mass % = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100
Mass by volume % = (mass of solute in g ÷ volume of solution in mL) × 100
Volume by volume % = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100
Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent
Solubility = maximum g of solute per 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature
commonMistakes: Dividing by the mass of the solvent instead of the mass of the solution in % m/m (10 g salt in 90 g water is 10%, not 11.1%).
Stating solubility without the temperature — solubility changes with temperature.
Thinking gases dissolve more in hot water — gases are less soluble as temperature rises.
Placing the ink spot below the solvent level in paper chromatography — it must be above, or the ink just dissolves into the solvent.
Using simple distillation for liquids whose boiling points are close (< 25 °C apart) — that needs fractional distillation.
Saying colloids settle or can be filtered — colloid particles pass through filter paper and don't settle; suspensions do.
Mixing up the emulsions: milk and vanishing cream are oil-in-water; butter and cold cream are water-in-oil.
Calling alloys compounds — they are mixtures (solid solutions) with variable composition.

Homogeneous = uniform (salt water, air); heterogeneous = visible parts (sand in water).
Solution < 1 nm; colloid 1–1000 nm; suspension > 1000 nm.
% m/m = solute mass ÷ solution mass × 100; also % m/v and % v/v.

Most solids: more soluble when hot; gases: less soluble when hot.
Crystallisation (slow cooling) gives purer product than evaporation.
Distillation: boiling points differ by ≥ 25 °C (acetone 56 °C and water 100 °C); fractional: < 25 °C.
Kannauj attars are made by traditional deg-bhapka distillation.
Chromatography: spot above solvent level; separates dyes in ink.
Separating funnel: water lower layer, mustard oil upper layer.
Sublimes: camphor, naphthalene, iodine, ammonium chloride.
Centrifugation: cream from milk, blood tests; alum makes mud settle; paneer by coagulating milk.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a solution, a colloid and a suspension?
faqs.a:
They differ in particle size:
- **Solution:** particles < 1 nm; homogeneous, clear, don't settle, pass through filter paper, no Tyndall effect (salt water)
- **Colloid:** particles 1–1000 nm; look uniform but are heterogeneous, don't settle, pass through filter paper, show Tyndall effect (milk)
- **Suspension:** particles > 1000 nm; heterogeneous, settle on standing, can be filtered, scatter light (muddy water)

faqs.q: When should I use distillation and when fractional distillation?
faqs.a: Both separate **miscible liquids** by boiling point. Use **simple distillation** when the boiling points differ by **25 °C or more** (e.g. acetone 56 °C and water 100 °C). Use **fractional distillation**, with a fractionating column, when the difference is **less than 25 °C** (e.g. separating gases of liquefied air or petroleum fractions).

faqs.q: Why is crystallisation better than evaporation for getting a pure solid?
faqs.a: Evaporating to dryness can **decompose or char** some solids (like sugar), and any soluble impurities dry onto the product. In crystallisation, the solution cools slowly, pure crystals form, and the impurities stay dissolved in the leftover liquid.

faqs.q: Is an alloy a mixture or a compound?
faqs.a: An alloy is a **mixture** — a homogeneous mixture or **solid solution**. Its composition can vary (brass can have different amounts of copper and zinc) and it shows properties of its components. It is not a compound because the metals are not combined in a fixed ratio by a chemical reaction.

faqs.q: Why can we see a torch beam in fog but not in salt water?
faqs.a: Fog is a **colloid**: its droplets are big enough (1–1000 nm) to **scatter light**, so the beam's path becomes visible — the **Tyndall effect**. Particles in a true solution like salt water are smaller than 1 nm and don't scatter light noticeably.

quiz.q: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
quiz.explain: In sand and water you can see separate parts; the others are uniform (homogeneous).

quiz.q: A colloid has particles of size:
quiz.explain: Solutions < 1 nm, colloids 1–1000 nm, suspensions > 1000 nm.

quiz.explain: The difference is 22 °C, less than 25 °C, so fractional distillation is needed.

quiz.q: In paper chromatography, the ink spot is placed above the solvent level because:
options: Otherwise the ink would just dissolve into the solvent in the jar
quiz.explain: If the spot is under the solvent, the dyes dissolve into the solvent pool instead of being carried up the paper.

quiz.q: Water and mustard oil are shaken and poured into a separating funnel. Which is true?
options: Water forms the lower layer and drains out first
quiz.explain: Water is denser, so it forms the lower layer and is run out through the stopcock first.

quiz.q: Which method is used in dairies to separate cream from milk?
quiz.explain: Spinning milk fast separates the lighter cream from the denser skimmed milk.

quiz.q: Which of these is a water-in-oil emulsion?
quiz.explain: Butter (and cold cream) are water-in-oil; milk and vanishing cream are oil-in-water. Salt water is a true solution.
